why: The tracker's on-disk layout has two readers since tick kya: internal/tick's
Store (Go, which owns the format and writes every record) and
cloud/factory/src/tick-membership.ts (the control plane, which reads one
record at a commit through GitHub's contents API to prove a requested wave's
ticks belong to the run's epic). This file is what both suites pin themselves
to, the same way worker-boot-contract.json pins the three readers of the
worker boot contract.
It matters more here than a parity fixture usually does, because of which way
the Worker's check fails: a tracker it cannot read ALLOWS the wave. So a
layout change landing in Go alone would not break the factory loudly — it
would silently turn every membership verdict into 'unreadable' and the check
would stop refusing anything, with both suites still green. This fixture is
what makes that change fail a test instead.
Since tick 8sm there is a WRITER on the TypeScript side too — the signal
funnel, which commits .tick/issues/<id>.json through the same contents API.
That half is pinned under 'written_by_the_control_plane' below, and it is a
stricter pin than the reader's: a reader that misunderstands the format
answers 'unreadable', while a writer that misunderstands it puts a malformed
record into someone's repository, which Go's own Store would have refused.
cloud/factory/src/tracker-write.ts mints an id and encodes a record that
Go's Store must accept unchanged, because the two write the same file in
the same repository — `tk create` on a laptop and a signal arriving at the
factory are the same act by different doors. Everything here is something
the TypeScript side hard-codes and Go owns.
Since tick hyi every signal that enters the factory is minted a trace id at
the edge, and that id is carried — never re-derived — onto the tick record,
the run record, the run's events and each worker container's log stream. It
is what joins 'a message arrived' to 'a container did this', which is the
join seven misdiagnosed Phase 2 runs did not have.
It crosses the Go/TS boundary in both directions, which is why it is pinned
here rather than declared twice. The control plane MINTS it and writes it
into the record (cloud/factory/src/trace.ts, tracker-write.ts); Go owns the
record format it lands in (internal/tick.Tick.TraceID), refuses a malformed
one in Validate, and reads it back in `tk cloud logs` and `tk cloud trace`.
A prefix or width that drifted in one language would produce records the
other refuses, with both suites green — the exact failure .tick/learnings.md
records under 'Cross-language parity'.
Omitted when empty, and empty is the COMMON case: a tick `tk create` filed
on a laptop is not a signal arriving at a front door, and minting an id for
it would claim a causal chain that does not exist.
The container half of the same id — the TICKS_TRACE_ID a worker boots with
and the banner heading its log stream — is pinned in worker-boot-contract.json
instead, beside the rest of the boot contract its three readers share.
Since tick la9 a signal does not become a tick when it arrives: it becomes a
DRAFT the operator accepts or discards in the channel. The design decision
that has to hold in BOTH languages is that a draft is not a tick in a special
state — it is not a tick. A tick record marked 'draft' would sit in
.tick/issues/ and be visible to `tk next`, `tk ready` and a wave's sweep,
leaving invisibility to whichever reader remembered to filter it.
So the pin is the status vocabulary itself. Go's Tick.Validate accepts
exactly the three values below and refuses everything else, which means a
draft-flavoured record is not expressible: a control plane that tried to
write one would produce a file `tk` refuses to read. The TypeScript half
commits 'committed_status' and nothing else, and reaching the writer at all
requires a draft id a human pressed (cloud/factory/src/signal-inbox.ts).
If a fourth status is ever added here, this fixture is what makes somebody
look at whether the gate still holds.
